text: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. But she had an Egyptian slave girl named Hagar,
and Sarai said to Abram, "Look, the LORD has kept me from bearing children. Go to my slave girl; perhaps I can build a family through her." And Abram listened to Sarai.
So Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her slave girl, and gave her to her husband Abram as a wife. This was after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan.
He went to Hagar, and she conceived. But when she saw that she was pregnant, she began to despise her mistress.

Then Sarai said to Abram, "This wrong done to me is your fault. I put my slave girl in your arms, and when she saw that she was pregnant, she began to despise me. Let the LORD judge between you and me!"

versions.text: Then Sarai said to Abram, "This wrong done to me is your fault. I put my slave girl in your arms, and now that she sees she is pregnant, she despises me. Let the LORD judge between you and me!"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verbs are narrative past ("she saw... I became slight in her eyes"). The shift to present tense ("now that she sees... she despises") breaks the tense sequence with "I put" earlier in the same sentence and is slightly awkward when read aloud.

text: Abram answered Sarai, "Your slave girl is in your hands. Do with her whatever you think best." So Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away from her.
The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness—the spring beside the road to Shur—
and he said, "Hagar, slave girl of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?" "I am running away from my mistress Sarai," she answered.
Then the angel of the LORD said to her, "Go back to your mistress and submit to her authority."
And the angel of the LORD said to her, "I will greatly increase your descendants; they will be too many to count."

The angel of the LORD also said to her, "You are pregnant, and you will give birth to a son. You shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction. [Footnote: Ishmael means "God hears."]

versions.text: The angel of the LORD also said to her, "You are pregnant, and you will give birth to a son. You shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.
versions.explanation: The wordplay between the name Ishmael and "the LORD has heard" is invisible in English; a brief footnote giving the meaning of the name would preserve the sense of the Hebrew for listeners.

text: He will be like a wild donkey of a man: his hand against everyone, and everyone's hand against him, and he will live at odds with all his kin."
So she gave a name to the LORD who had spoken to her: "You are the God who sees me," for she said, "Have I really seen him and lived, the One who sees me?"
That is why the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered. [Footnote: Beer-lahai-roi means "well of the Living One who sees me."]

versions.text: That is why the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered.
versions.explanation: The transliterated name carries no meaning for English hearers, and it directly echoes Hagar's confession in the previous verse. A short footnote with the meaning links the two verses.

text: Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named the son she bore him Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore him Ishmael.
